facts.claim: GIA distinguishes ring settings (how a gemstone is secured, such as prongs or a bezel) from setting styles (the overall arrangement of stones, such as solitaire, halo or three-stone); the same setting type can produce very different looks.

A solitaire features a single centre gemstone with little or no additional decoration, putting full visual emphasis on the stone's shape, size and quality; it is often paired with prong or bezel settings.
GIA says solitaires are valued for a clean, timeless look and versatility, pair easily with a wide range of wedding bands, and suit both traditional and contemporary tastes.
GIA says round brilliant and princess cut centre stones flatter almost any finger length and shape.

A halo is a prong- or bezel-set centre stone surrounded by a ring of smaller accent stones, which adds sparkle and frames the centre so it can appear larger; GIA says the centre stone can appear to be the size of the halo.

Halos can use coloured gemstones or fancy-colour diamonds to intensify or contrast with the centre stone, and range from a subtle frame to a large halo that significantly increases the ring's footprint.

Because halo rings contain many small stones they may need more maintenance to keep stones secure and clean, and GIA notes the prongs on halo designs tend to wear out faster, so the ring should be routinely checked by a jeweller.

A hidden halo is a row of small accent stones set beneath the centre stone, visible mainly from the side; from above the ring keeps a solitaire-like look. Definition only, from jewellers' pages (no gemmological body source found); describe in our own words, no endorsement.
A three-stone ring has a centre gemstone flanked by two smaller side stones, which may match the centre (adding visual width) or differ in shape or colour to complement or contrast with it.
GIA says the three-stone design symbolises 'yesterday, today and tomorrow' (its settings guide phrases it as a couple's past, present and future).
GIA calls the three-stone design balanced and says it works well no matter what the size of the hand or finger.
facts.conflicts: Brief says three-stone 'works well on longer fingers and wider hands'; GIA says it suits any hand or finger size. Use the GIA framing.

facts.claim: GIA notes three-stone rings may pose resizing challenges if the side stones are built into the band, and need occasional care to keep stones secure. (Extracted from the settings guide's three-stone section by page summary; wording to be paraphrased, not quoted.)

Toi et moi ('you and me' in French) sets two gemstones side by side; GIA says it remains popular in both antique-inspired and contemporary rings and that the two stones are said to symbolise two lives intertwining.
In 1796 Napoleon Bonaparte gave his future empress, Josephine, a sapphire and diamond toi et moi ring for their engagement.

GIA notes toi et moi rings often need periodic checks to keep the stones secure, and resizing can be more complicated depending on the arrangement of the stones. (Page-summary extraction; paraphrase.)

An east-west setting turns an elongated stone (GIA's example is an oval) horizontally across the finger instead of vertically; GIA calls it a contemporary, fashion-forward look, especially striking in minimalist or bezel-set styles, and says it can make a modest stone appear larger and more distinctive.
GIA says elongated shapes (marquise, oval, rectangular, pear) have a 'north-south axis' that can accentuate the length of the finger when set the traditional way.
GIA notes radiant cuts are usually set north-south but the east-west orientation is gaining popularity.
facts.source: https://4cs.gia.edu/en-us/blog/page/6/ (excerpt of 'Buying a Radiant Cut Engagement Ring')

facts.claim: A cluster places several small diamonds of similar size next to each other, maximising sparkle and giving the illusion of a single, much larger diamond; GIA adds that cluster settings have lots of metal, which helps safeguard the stones.

GIA's settings guide says cluster designs let smaller stones create a bold overall look and can combine different shapes and colours, but may need regular maintenance to keep stones in place. (Page-summary extraction; paraphrase.)
GIA suggests cluster-set styles can make a bold statement on larger fingers.
GIA defines antique jewellery as made more than 100 years ago, and vintage as not contemporary but not old enough to be antique. (Page-summary extraction; paraphrase.)
For an Edwardian-style ring GIA suggests vintage motifs such as scrollwork, milgrain and engraving, and describes milgrain and latticework as giving the lacy look of that era.
GIA warns that prongs on antique and vintage rings can weaken with years of wear; thin or worn prongs cannot hold the stone as securely, making it vulnerable to loss.
Art Deco was a prominent jewellery style of the 1920s and 1930s, defined by geometric patterns and abstract designs using diamonds and gems in contrasting colours.
Art Deco designers used triangles, squares, rectangles and circles, and favoured shapes such as emerald cuts and baguettes; GIA describes the look as contrast, balance and symmetry.

Black and white (diamonds with black onyx or black enamel) is a telltale Art Deco contrast; platinum was favoured for its strength, tarnish resistance and malleability, and pavé evolved during this period.

GIA: 'If you love a simple, yet bold style, then Art Deco vintage engagement rings would suit your taste.' GIA also notes it may be more practical to design a new ring using Art Deco motifs than to seek an original from the period.
Pavé sets many small diamonds closely into tapered holes in the metal, creating an uninterrupted surface of sparkle that can make the centre stone look larger.

GIA says pavé-set diamonds are typically very secure, but if one falls out it is harder for a bench jeweller to replace; it advises avoiding pavé on the underside of the shank, where friction makes stones easier to lose or damage.
Halo and pavé designs may need more maintenance, and pavé-set bands can be harder to resize because adjusting the ring may disturb the small stones (re-checked from sister pack fact_26).

A bezel holds the stone with a thin metal rim around its girdle; GIA says bezels resist chips and everyday wear, their smooth edges are less likely to catch on clothing or gloves, and they are a practical choice for people who work with their hands or have an active lifestyle (re-checked from sister pack fact_01, fact_02).

Bezels cover more of the stone's edge and let slightly less light in than prongs, but give a clean, modern look; GIA adds the bezel can make the stone's circumference appear larger (re-checked from sister fact_03).
A split shank is a band that separates on either side of the main stone.
GIA notes a split shoulder band set with small diamonds can make a ring look a lot larger.
GIA says a thin band can make a diamond look larger while a thick band can overshadow it; broader bands give a bold, modern presence.
Channel-set and bar-set rings can be difficult to resize, especially when the stones extend far around the band (re-checked from sister fact_20, fact_23).

Jewellers state a full eternity band generally cannot be resized because stones occupy the metal that would be cut and rejoined. Jeweller page, used as context only; GIA states the general principle (fact above), not this specific claim.

GIA describes a bypass ring as a style where the band overlaps instead of completing the circle, notes bypass rings were popular in the Victorian era, and shows designs that combine bypass with toi et moi.

Mohs hardness measures scratch resistance only; durability depends on hardness, toughness and stability. Sapphire and ruby (corundum) are 9 on the Mohs scale, diamond 10 (re-checked from sister fact_29, fact_32).
Emerald is 7.5 to 8 on the Mohs scale but is not a tough gem, often has surface-reaching fractures and is often treated with oil or resin (sister fact_33).
GIA's coloured gemstone guide says spinel, morganite, zircon, tsavorite and tourmaline can be worn daily with care (sister fact_34).
GIA says bezels, halos and other protective settings can play an important role in preventing chipping or cracking of coloured gemstones.
GIA says larger fingers can carry a larger sapphire, ruby or tourmaline, and long, slender fingers suit larger diamonds and coloured gems.

GIA hand and finger guidance: a simple design usually suits shorter fingers (complex designs can overwhelm); smaller rings and simple designs suit petite fingers; long, slender fingers can carry the widest range including larger stones and stacked bands; a medium to wide band suits larger fingers as long as it is comfortable; the wedding band worn alongside will affect the overall look. Source uses gendered language; rewrite neutrally.
A higher setting can make a stone look bigger but is more likely to snag and more susceptible to damage; lower profiles are less likely to snag.
GIA suggests having prongs checked every six months, or at least yearly (sister fact_11).

GIA advises removing the ring before gardening or other risky activities (sister fact_28) and removing diamond jewellery before chlorinated pools or hot tubs, as chlorine can erode some alloys and loosen prongs (sister fact_39).

GIA advises packing jewellery in carry-on rather than checked luggage and telling your insurer your travel dates (sister fact_40); and checking that a policy covers loss and damage as well as theft (sister fact_42).
GIA notes some popular destinations and activities can be hard on jewellery and suggests leaving fragile pieces or softer gems at home or packing them carefully (sister fact_44).
GIA suggests professional cleaning once or twice a year, and home cleaning with mild soap, warm water and a soft brush; a clean stone looks brighter.

insider_details.detail: Halo, pavé and cluster designs all rely on many small stones, so build a jeweller check (GIA suggests every six months, or at least yearly) into the calendar before the wedding trip, not after.

If the ring may need resizing later (fingers change, or it was bought as a surprise), favour designs with plain metal at the back: GIA flags pavé, channel, bar, three-stone and toi et moi designs as harder to resize, and full eternity bands are generally treated as not resizable.
For a surprise proposal, round and princess centres and the three-stone layout are the safest bets for an unknown hand, because GIA says they flatter almost any finger.

Choosing an emerald or another softer coloured stone for its meaning? Pair it with a protective bezel or halo and plan to swap to a plain band for snorkelling, pool and beach days, since GIA rates emerald as not a tough gem and advises removing rings before chlorine and rough activities.

Sapphire and ruby are 9 on the Mohs scale, second only to diamond, which is why GIA lists them among coloured stones that cope with daily wear; Napoleon's 1796 sapphire and diamond toi et moi is the classic precedent for pairing them.
Fly with the ring in carry-on, tell the insurer the travel dates and check the policy covers loss and damage overseas, not only theft.

open_questions.question: Brief's open question for the fact-checker answered: gemstone durability is GIA-sourced (fact_40 to fact_43); eternity resizing is GIA-sourced only as the general principle (fact_37, fact_31), so write 'stones running far around the band make resizing difficult, and full eternity bands are often not resizable; ask before you buy' without figures.

Several brief 'who it suits' lines are opinion (halo for shorter fingers, east-west widening, split shank for slim fingers). Three are listed as verify_items; where GIA disagrees (halo, three-stone), follow GIA. Facts tagged 'page-summary extraction' (fact_12, fact_15, fact_20, fact_22) must be paraphrased, not quoted.
GIA's hand guidance (fact_45) and toi et moi/three-stone pages use gendered wording ('her finger', 'brides'); rewrite as 'the wearer'.

assumptions: Fast mode, 15-minute budget: sources limited to GIA 4Cs pages plus two jeweller pages for definitions. No museum (V&A, Met) page used; GIA's Art Deco and vintage pages cover era and motifs.
Hidden halo, bypass and 'contemporary' styles are design vocabulary; descriptions in our own words do not need a [[VERIFY]] beyond the sourced definitions.
Photography and destination-light lines (art deco in Mediterranean light, hidden halo in side profile) are planner advice, not fact claims.
